blocks.html: Every day we use the Internet for UPI payments, online classes, DigiLocker, train bookings and hospital reports. The same connection that makes life easy also lets criminals try to steal data, money or identity, or to damage systems.
Cyber security is the practice of protecting computers, networks, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.
It rests on three goals, often called the CIA triad:

rows: Only authorised people can see the data
Only you and the bank can see your balance
Data is not changed without permission
Nobody can secretly change your exam marks
Systems and data are available when needed
The result website does not crash on result day

blocks.html: Malware (MALicious softWARE) is any program written to harm a computer, steal data or take control of a system.

blocks.html: Virus vs worm: a virus needs a host file and a user action (opening the file). A worm needs neither and spreads by itself through the network.

items.html: Downloading software, games or movies from untrusted websites.
Opening email attachments or WhatsApp files from unknown senders.
Clicking links in fake messages ("You won ₹10 lakh! Click here").
Plugging in infected pen drives.
Weaknesses in outdated software that has not been updated.
Installing pirated software or unofficial app files (APKs).

blocks.html: Signs of infection: the computer slows down suddenly, strange pop-ups appear, files go missing or get renamed, programs start on their own, or friends receive messages you did not send.
Antivirus software detects, blocks and removes malware. Common methods:

rows: Compares files with a database of known malware "signatures" (patterns)
Accurate for known malware, but cannot catch brand-new malware until the database is updated
Looks for suspicious behaviour, such as a program trying to encrypt many files quickly
Can catch new malware, but sometimes raises false alarms
Runs a suspicious file in a safe, isolated area and watches what it does
Scans files as they are downloaded or opened

blocks.html: Good habit: keep the antivirus and the operating system updated, and scan pen drives before opening them.

Spam is unwanted bulk messages: email, SMS or WhatsApp. It is used for advertising, and often for fraud and malware. Email services filter spam into a separate folder. Never click links or download attachments from spam.
A cookie is a small text file that a website stores in your browser to remember you: your login, your language choice, the items in your shopping cart.

items.html: First-party cookies come from the site you visit. They are mostly useful.
Third-party cookies come from other companies (often advertisers) and track you across websites, which raises privacy concerns.

blocks.html: You can view, block and delete cookies in your browser settings. On a shared or cyber- café computer, always log out and clear cookies.

Encrypted with TLS: looks like nonsense to eavesdroppers
All logins, banking, UPI and shopping

blocks.html: HTTPS also uses a digital certificate to prove the website is really who it says it is.
A firewall is a security system (hardware, software or both) that sits between a trusted network and the Internet. It checks every packet against a set of rules and allows or blocks it.

items.html: Network firewall: protects a whole LAN, usually built into the router or a separate device.
Host-based firewall: software on one computer, such as Windows Defender Firewall.

blocks.caption: Figure 12.2 · a firewall between the Internet and a school LAN

blocks.html: Example rules: allow web traffic (port 443) out; block all incoming connections that were not requested; block a known bad IP address.

lessons.title: 12.7 Cyber law and reporting in India

items.html: Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 (amended in 2008): India's main cyber law. It gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, and defines cyber offences such as hacking (Section 66), identity theft (Section 66C) and cheating by impersonation using computers (Section 66D).
CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team): the national agency that responds to cyber security incidents.
Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023: protects people's personal data and sets duties for organisations that collect it.
Call the National Cyber Crime Helpline 1930, especially for financial fraud. Call immediately: reporting quickly gives the best chance of stopping the money.
File a complaint on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal: cybercrime.gov.in.
Keep the evidence: screenshots, transaction IDs, phone numbers, links and emails.

Encryption turns readable text (plaintext) into unreadable text (ciphertext) using a key. Only someone with the key can decrypt it. HTTPS uses very strong encryption. The Caesar cipher, used by Julius Caesar, is the simplest example: shift every letter by a fixed number of places.
+ 26 before % 26 keeps the result positive when the key is negative (for decryption). A
Caesar cipher is easy to break, because there are only 25 possible keys, so it is used only for learning. Real systems use algorithms such as AES and RSA.
Limiting wrong attempts stops attackers from simply trying every password (a brute- force attack).

Real systems never store the password itself. They store a hash: a one-way scrambled value calculated from the password with a special algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2. When you log in, the system hashes what you type and compares the two hashes. If the database is stolen, the attacker gets only the hashes, not the passwords.

items.html: Cyber security protects systems and data. Its goals are Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability (the CIA triad).

Malware: a virus needs a host file and a user action; a worm spreads by itself; a Trojan looks useful but harms; ransomware encrypts files for money; spyware watches you; adware shows ads; a keylogger records keys.
Malware spreads through untrusted downloads, attachments, links, pen drives, pirated software and outdated systems.
Antivirus uses signature-based, heuristic and sandbox detection. Keep it updated.
Spam = unwanted bulk messages. Cookies = small files that websites store (third- party cookies track you). HTTPS encrypts web traffic (port 443, lock icon). A firewall filters traffic by rules.
White-hat hackers work with permission; black-hat crackers commit crimes. Attacks include DoS/DDoS, snooping, eavesdropping and phishing (also vishing and smishing).
Safe habits: strong unique passwords, 2FA, never share OTPs or PINs, check URLs, update, back up, avoid public Wi-Fi for banking.
India: the IT Act 2000 (amended 2008), CERT-In and the DPDP Act 2023. Report cybercrime on 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in.
